business_model: Organism-engineering-as-a-service platform, R&D-partnership and licensing revenue, long development horizon

historical_evidence.company: Founded 2008 by five MIT-trained scientists/engineers, building a platform ('foundry') for designing and manufacturing custom organisms for industrial, agricultural, and other applications.
historical_evidence.market: Large, thesis-dependent long-term market opportunity (the 'bioeconomy') with very few direct public comparables at this scale, making market-size and competitive-intensity assessment inherently more speculative than for a typical software company.
historical_evidence.team: Founding team of five PhD-level scientists/engineers from MIT with deep, directly relevant academic/technical domain expertise in synthetic biology — a strong Founder-Market-Fit and Technical-Capability signal by credential, though 'has this specific team commercialized a platform business before' remained an open question at this stage.
historical_evidence.product: A biological-engineering platform intended to reduce the cost and time of designing custom organisms, monetized primarily through R&D partnerships and program fees with corporate/industrial partners rather than a conventional per-unit product sale.
historical_evidence.execution: Raised $275M in Series D funding in December 2017, valuing the company at over $1 billion, from a notably sophisticated investor group including Viking Global, Y Combinator's Continuity Fund, Cascade Investment (Bill Gates' investment vehicle), and General Atlantic — a strong signal of late-stage, technically-literate capital conviction in the underlying platform thesis.
historical_evidence.traction: No specific program-count, partnership-revenue, or program-fee figures were found in the contemporaneous sources reviewed for the December 2017 snapshot.
historical_evidence.financial: The scale of the raise ($275M) relative to the company's long-horizon R&D-platform model implies a long capital runway was being built deliberately, consistent with a deeptech thesis where near-term revenue is not the primary near-term proof point — a structurally different Financial-Health read than a typical SaaS or marketplace company would warrant at the same nominal funding stage.

normalized_facts.source: TechCrunch ("valuing the company at over $1 billion")

sources.title: Ginkgo Bioworks secures $275 million in Series D, valuing the company at over $1 billion
Leveraging the Power of Biology for Manufacturing: Ginkgo Bioworks Raises $275 Million in Series D Funding

future_outcome.outcome_type: went public via SPAC, subsequent valuation decline
future_outcome.outcome_summary: Ginkgo Bioworks continued raising large private rounds (reaching a $4.2B valuation by a September 2019 Series E) before going public via a SPAC merger in 2021 at a roughly $15B valuation; its public-market valuation subsequently declined substantially in the years following, with ongoing public debate about whether the platform thesis had been overvalued relative to demonstrated near-term revenue.

benchmark_notes.why_included: A deliberate deeptech/non-SaaS stress test for the methodology, chosen specifically because it does not fit the standard SaaS-metric evidence pattern (no MRR/ARR, no customer-growth-rate, no NRR) that most of this benchmark portfolio's companies do have available. Tests whether SIE's Financial Health and Traction pillars correctly recognize a long-horizon R&D-platform business model as a legitimate, different evidentiary shape rather than either forcing SaaS-style metrics that don't apply or defaulting the whole company to low confidence purely because familiar metrics are absent.
benchmark_notes.known_ambiguities: Even at the time, sophisticated observers held genuinely divided views on whether Ginkgo's platform thesis justified its valuation — this is not a case where a single 'obviously correct' contemporaneous read exists, and the record intentionally reflects that genuine ambiguity in the Promising/High-Uncertainty tier rather than forcing a more confident label in either direction.
benchmark_notes.evidence_limitations: No program-count, partnership-revenue, or other traction-adjacent figures specific to the December 2017 snapshot were located in the sources reviewed; this benchmark is expected to produce a Traction pillar that is largely Unavailable or Not-Applicable given the business model, which is itself the intended test.
